title: Classical Languages of India (Shastriya Bhasha)
answer: The Government of India grants 'Classical Language' status to languages with high antiquity of recorded history over 1,500–2,000 years, rich ancient literature/epics, and original literary tradition. The classical languages include Tamil (2004), Sanskrit (2005), Telugu (2008), Kannada (2008), Malayalam (2013), and Odia (2014).
highlights: Chronology of Recognition: 1) Tamil (2004), 2) Sanskrit (2005), 3) Telugu (2008), 4) Kannada (2008), 5) Malayalam (2013), 6) Odia (2014)
2024 Expansions: Union Cabinet approved classical status for Marathi, Pali, Prakrit, Assamese, and Bengali in October 2024

Key Criteria: High antiquity of early texts/recorded history exceeding 1,500–2,000 years; valuable heritage of ancient literature considered by generations of speakers as priceless; distinct and not borrowed from another speech community

title: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage Elements from India
answer: UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity includes prominent Indian traditions such as Vedic Chanting (2008), Ramlila (2008), Yoga (2016), Kumbh Mela (2017), Durga Puja in Kolkata (2021), and Garba of Gujarat (2023).
highlights: Vedic Chanting (2008): Traditional sacred oral recitation of Vedic mantras with pitch and accent accuracy
Ramlila (2008): Dramatic folk re-enactment of the life of Lord Rama based on the Ramcharitmanas
Kumbh Mela (2017): World's largest peaceful congregation of pilgrims, held cyclically at Prayagraj, Haridwar, Ujjain, and Nashik
Yoga (2016): Ancient Indian physical, mental, and spiritual discipline
Durga Puja in Kolkata (2021): Annual socio-cultural and religious festival featuring artistic pandals and clay idol immersion
Garba of Gujarat (2023): Ritualistic ceremonial circle dance performed during the Hindu festival of Navratri

title: Legendary Indian Authors & Landmark Masterpieces
answer: Prominent Indian literary stalwarts include Munshi Premchand ('Upanyas Samrat', author of 'Godan' and 'Gaban'), Mirza Ghalib (master of the Urdu Ghazal and 'Diwan-e-Ghalib'), Ramdhari Singh Dinkar (Rashtrakavi, author of 'Rashmirathi' and 'Urvashi'), and Kalidasa (ancient Sanskrit dramatist who composed 'Abhijnanashakuntalam' and 'Meghaduta').
highlights: Munshi Premchand (Hindi/Urdu): 'Godan' (1936 epic novel on Indian peasant plight), 'Gaban', 'Karmabhoomi', 'Sevasadan', 'Mansarovar' short stories
Harivansh Rai Bachchan (Hindi): 'Madhushala' (1935 poetic masterpiece), 'Neele Jheel', 'Kya Bhooloon Kya Yaad Karoon'
Ramdhari Singh Dinkar (Hindi): 'Rashmirathi' (poetic retelling of Karna from Mahabharata), 'Urvashi' (1972 Jnanpith Award winner), 'Kurukshetra'
Mirza Ghalib (Urdu/Persian): Preeminent 19th-century Mughal-era poet famous for his ghazals and letters compiled in 'Diwan-e-Ghalib'
Kalidasa (Sanskrit): Greatest classical Sanskrit playwright and poet ('Abhijnanashakuntalam', 'Meghaduta', 'Raghuvamsha', 'Kumarasambhava')

title: Figures of Speech & Literary Devices Reference
answer: Figures of speech are rhetorical devices used to add emphasis, freshness of expression, or clarity: Simile (explicit comparison using 'like' or 'as'), Metaphor (direct implicit comparison asserting one thing is another), Personification (attributing human characteristics to non-human entities), Alliteration (repetition of initial consonant sounds), and Oxymoron (pairing contradictory terms like 'deafening silence').
highlights: Simile: 'As brave as a lion', 'Shone like diamonds' (explicit comparison with 'as' or 'like')
Metaphor: 'Time is a thief', 'The world is a stage' (asserts identity between two disparate things)
Personification: 'The wind whispered through the trees', 'Opportunity knocks at the door'
Alliteration: 'Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers' (repetition of initial consonant sounds)
Oxymoron: 'Deafening silence', 'Bitter sweet', 'Living dead' (side-by-side contradictory terms)
Hyperbole: 'I have told you a million times', 'I am so hungry I could eat a horse' (intentional extreme exaggeration)

title: Poetic Forms (Sonnet, Haiku, Limerick) & Literary Genres
answer: A Sonnet is a 14-line lyric poem written in iambic pentameter (Shakespearean format: 3 quatrains + 1 rhyming couplet, ABAB CDCD EFEF GG; Petrarchan format: Octave + Sestet, ABBAABBA CDECDE). A Haiku is a traditional Japanese unrhymed 3-line poetic form with a 5-7-5 syllable structure focusing on nature or seasons.
highlights: Shakespearean / English Sonnet: 14 lines, iambic pentameter, rhyme scheme ABAB CDCD EFEF GG, ending with a volta/turn and resolving couplet
Petrarchan / Italian Sonnet: 14 lines divided into an 8-line Octave (proposing problem/question, ABBAABBA) and 6-line Sestet (resolution, CDECDE)
Haiku: 3-line Japanese poem consisting of 17 syllables in total (5 in first line, 7 in second line, 5 in third line) with a seasonal word (kigo)
Limerick: Humorous 5-line poem with an AABBA rhyme scheme and anapestic rhythm
Epic: Extended narrative poem celebrating heroic feats (Homer's 'Iliad' and 'Odyssey', Vyasa's 'Mahabharata', Valmiki's 'Ramayana')

title: Classical Languages of India — Complete List & Criteria
answer: India officially recognizes 11 Classical Languages having high antiquity (early texts recorded over 1,500–2,000 years), ancient literature considered valuable heritage, and original literary tradition: Tamil (declared 2004), Sanskrit (2005), Kannada (2008), Telugu (2008), Malayalam (2013), Odia (2014), and expanded in October 2024 to include Marathi, Pali, Prakrit, Assamese, and Bengali.
highlights: Tamil: First language to receive Classical status in 2004 (Sangam literature dating back to 300 BCE)
Sanskrit: Declared in 2005 (Vedas, Upanishads, Panini's Ashtadhyayi grammar (~500 BCE))
Kannada & Telugu: Declared in 2008 (Kavirajamarga in Kannada, Nannayya's Mahabharata in Telugu)
Malayalam (2013) and Odia (2014)
New Additions (October 2024): Marathi, Pali, Prakrit, Assamese, and Bengali approved by Union Cabinet
